#4325. Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health

The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events

To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable

One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."

Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.

The other event is the Candleberry Banquet Project, which requires you to donate items found on the surface (including Candleberries).

While on the subject, the new update also kicks off a new Raider Deck (battle pass). Available from December 26, The Goalie Raider Deck is pretty much what you’d expect. You’ll find several pages of cosmetic and useful items. The new Deck will be available to all players for free.

#4321. Arc Raiders' latest patch adds two of the most requested features, but kills Cred hoarding

The last major Arc Raiders update of the year has arrived, bringing several big new features to the game, but not without some bad news.

Embark has just rolled out patch 1.7.0 for Arc Raiders players everywhere. This is a significant patch for the extraction shooter for a number of reasons, not least of which because it kicks off a series of events under the Cold Snap banner, which introduces a new conditions to the game’s maps.

Dig deeper into the patch notes, however, and you’ll find even more to get excited about, including features players have been asking for since the game’s first public test.

To start with, today’s update finally adds an option toggle aiming down sights. This is especially relevant for PC players, most of whom play shooters with an ADS toggle, rather than hold. Another often requested feature has been the ability to reset the game’s skill tree.

This is now available for the cost of 2,000 Coins per skill point. It goes without saying that you’re going to need a whole lot of money to reset the entire thing, but it’s a useful option to have when you want to alter your path.

The next change is one that’s going to ruffle a lot of feathers. Arc Raiders now has a soft Cred cap of 800. This is now clearly shown on your Wallet screen, and the developer said the cap is necessary to prevent players from using their accumulated Cred to unlock new Raider Decks immediately after release.

The good news is that this won’t affect the Cred you may already have, but going forward, 800 is the most you can hold at any point. You’ll also notice that Shani has more stuff for you to buy with Cred, in case you want another way to spend what you have.

Patch 1.7.0 also brings a few other additions - and makes some changes - that are worth highlighting. You can now customise your Raider Tool, which likely means we’re going to see Raider Tool cosmetics going forward.

Speaking of items, the Aphelion weapon blueprint has been moved to Stella Montis, so you won’t be able to get it from taking down the Matriarch. The Bettina, and Rattler have both seen some balance changes.

The Bettina’s durability will now degrade a lot slower per shot, making it take 26 magazines to fully deplete durability. The base magazine size has been increased to 22, and the reload time has been cut to 4.5 seconds. Embark says this should make the weapon more viable in PvP, while also allowing it to stand on its own without the need for players bring a secondary weapon.

As for the Rattler, the only change it gets is an increase to its magazine size from 10 to 12. The idea is to make it about as effective as a Stitcher or Kettle at close ranges when it comes to PvP encounters.

And, of course, it wouldn’t be a big Arc Raiders patch without some tweaks to the game’s Arc enemies. This time, the Shredder gets all the love. The menacing unit now moves faster, turns more sharply and doesn’t get knocked back as much when shot.

The Shredder’s head now has more health, too, meaning you won’t be able to shoot it off early and confuse it. In general, the Arc unit should be smarter, especially when navigating narrow spaces. Finally, the Shredder now activates faster upon detecting (and being attacked by) players.

Beyond that, the main menu has seen a few changes to highlight ongoing events, make certain announcements quieter, make it easier to track Raider Quests and more. There’s a lot more in this update, too, such as changes to footstep loudness, several tweaks to loot and the value of certain items, and more besides. You’ll find the full change log on the official website.

#4320. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

Materials provided by Semmelweis University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4319. Laid-Off Id Software Employees Form their Own Studio, Hidden Horses

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

2026 has been home to a swath of large-scale layoffs throughout the gaming industry, mostly in the western sector. A statistically-significant portion of these layoffs have come from Microsoft, which has been systematically pruning many of its subsidiaries, including some of its highest-profile studios like id Software and Bethesda. Obviously, this is terrible for the many, many developers who worked for those studios, but some of those same developers have decided to turn this pinch into a chance.

Xbox cut 3,200 jobs. The developers who lost theirs explain what that actually means for the games that were supposed to come next.

Today, a coalition of developers who were specifically laid off from id Software following their work on Doom: The Dark Ages announced the formation of their new independent studio: Hidden Horses. If that name is a reference to something, I don’t know what it is, but what this studio may lack in readily-apparent branding, it more than makes up for in the crew of talented, highly-experienced developers it consists of.

According to Hidden Horses’s newly-created website, this independent studio wants to make games “like it was done in the 90’s,” with an emphasis on carefully hand-crafted gaming experiences tailored by longtime industry veterans. The studio’s first project is already in progress, with plans to bring it to life via crowdfunding in the near future.

While these industry vets have lost the ample funding that comes with a major backer like Microsoft, they have, in turn, gained substantial freedom in how they pursue their projects. This is one of the stated benefits of the studio’s formation, as outlined on the “How We Work” section of the Hidden Horses website.

“The company was created as a developer run and owned studio,” the page reads. “This allows us to pursue fun and creativity in our games, unencumbered by short-term thinking or chasing market trends.”

They have gained substantial freedom in how they pursue their projects.

The team considers this structure optimal because helps them make games right, rather than make them quickly, creating new and interesting gameplay concepts rather than trying to flip half-baked products for a quick buck. The team is firmly of the belief that, despite changes in the industry and players, there is still very much a demand for the kinds of carefully-designed games that they’re accustomed to creating.

After being cut off by its previous publisher, Romero Games has secured a fresh bout of funding and refocused with a smaller dev team.

The page also notes that the studio will be run democratically, with input from every member of the team on all important business decisions, all to ensure nobody gets left out in the cold. “We do this not only because we think it is fair, but because we think it is a better way to run a business.”

Despite having just formed, Hidden Horses already has irons in the fire. On the “Our First Project” page of the website, the studio outlines its plans for its very first game development project. This game, titled Danger Pay, will be a “high-octane single-player FPS” set in a malevolent, futuristic game show in a manner reminiscent of Smash TV and The Running Man.

“Our game will focus on classic FPS gameplay, awesome weapons, crazy enemies, and will be highly optimized.”

Of course, financial backing for an entirely new game project doesn’t come out of nowhere, which is why the plan for this first project is to fund it via Kickstarter. A page for Danger Pay has already been created, though there’s no word yet on when the campaign will actually begin.

“We believe that the community around the type of games we have helped develop is robust, and we invite all supporters to join us in trying to create something special,” the Kickstarter description reads. “This will include the typical things needed to start a business and finance a game's development - licenses, hardware, healthcare, etc. Our goal will be based around the timeline of our first project and associated costs.”

You can now experience Wyldheart, the upcoming co-op RPG from former AAA developers, for yourself.

#4318. It’s official: Battlefield 6 is 2025's best-selling game, but Black Ops 7 still managed to be November’s top-seller

2025 will be remembered for many things, but in the ultra-competitive games industry, it’s going to be thought of as the year Battlefield 6 did what many thought couldn’t happen.

Circan’s November 2025 video game sales report has easily been one of the most anticipated. For one, November is always one of the most lucrative for the games industry, but this year in particular has seen several major hits - including new entries in two rival series.

We’re talking, of course, about Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 the latest releases in their respective multiplayer shooter series. The decades-old fight to claim the top spot has long been won by Call of Duty, but the latest Battlefield has achieved what many thought was impossible.

Cricana’s report covers spending on video game software, hardware, and accessories in the U.S. November 2025 saw spending fall by 4% compared to November 2024, bringing in a total of $5.9 billion.

Software technically saw growth during the month, but declines in hardware, and accessories were mainly responsible for the drop in overall spending. Black Ops 7 continued Call of Duty’s 18-Year Streak in topping sales in its launch month.

However, this year’s game did not also top the year-to-date charts, something the series has done consistently, and more than any other top-selling game each year - with rare exceptions. Battlefield 6 is firmly in the lead there, cementing its claim as 2025’s best-selling title. Black Ops 7, fittingly, occupies in the #7 spot there.

Separately from the best-selling game title fight, November has actually been one of the worst for the industry in terms of hardware sales. The report notes that the three major platform holders - Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo have all seen their hardware sales decline.

Spending on hardware during November amounted to only $695 million, a massive 27% decline compared to November 2024. According to the report, that’s the worst dollar amount total for any November since 2005, when it comes to hardware specifically. All three current-gen consoles totaled 1.6 million units sold, which Circana also notes is the lowest for any November since 1995.

This all doesn’t bode especially well for the industry. November has always been a key holiday shopping month, but it’s clear the constantly rising console prices - and already high game prices - have had a big impact.

#4316. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#4313. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4311. Jordan Esports Federation signs MoU with King Hussein Business Park to host more events

Priya Venkatesh has been following the money in esports since before brand deals were considered legitimate marketing. She got pulled into the scene through competitive fighting games and eventually found herself more interested in the contracts and partnerships behind the tournaments than the matches themselves. These days she focuses on how brands navigate esports sponsorships, where the smart money is going, and which deals are actually built to last versus the ones that look good in a press release.

The Jordan Esports Federation (JEF) has signed a memorandum of understanding with King Hussein Business Park (KHBP) in Amman, giving the national body a formal framework to stage more tournaments and events at the site it already calls home.

KHBP announced the deal on Sunday in a statement published on its website. Prince Omar bin Faisal, who is President of the JEF, attended the signing.

Under the MoU, the federation and the business park will jointly host and organise specialised competitions on the KHBP campus. They will also receive the international delegations and official guests that travel to those events. Beyond the competitive side, the two organisations plan to cooperate on media and marketing, look at shared education, training and community projects, and swap knowledge and expertise.

Neither party has disclosed financial terms or the length of the agreement.

KHBP CEO Eng. Ammar Ezzeddin presented the MoU as part of the park’s wider ambitions. “This partnership builds on our ongoing efforts to create an enabling environment for institutions, initiatives and high-potential sectors, and to establish KHBP as a hub for innovation and technology,” he said.

He added: “We look forward to helping the sector thrive and to hosting more tournaments and events that put Jordanian talent in the spotlight and raise the Kingdom’s profile in this field.”

JEF Vice President Hazem Bawab focused on the competitive and grassroots goals. “This partnership is a significant step in our drive to develop the esports industry in Jordan and elevate the standard of local, regional and international competitions and activities,” he said.

Bawab continued: “We look forward to drawing on the setup and capabilities that KHBP offers to scale our work, nurture young talent and launch joint programmes that help the industry grow and encourage greater participation.”

The deal formalises a relationship that already exists on the ground. According to The Esports Radar, the JEF, which is the government recognised regulator for esports in the country, is based at the park in West Amman.

A lot of that work happens at THE ARC, the arena and gaming dome inside the park. The same report lists past events there including the fourth Arab Esports League, a Women’s Esports Championship and Red Bull Login, which doubled as Jordan’s national final stage in Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2. The venue is also an incubation centre supported by the federation and the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship, and runs training camps for players hoping to turn professional.

KHBP has been a destination for esports investment for some time. In 2024, lounge operator True Gamers announced plans for an esports venue in Jordan at the business park, a project in which its CPO publicly thanked the JEF and Prince Omar.

The timing also puts Amman in the industry spotlight. PocketGamer.biz points out that Pocket Gamer Connects Jordan takes place on 7 and 8 November, bringing many of the region’s games industry stakeholders to the city later this week.

#4310. Jensen Huang’s Departure from NVIDIA Sparks Hope of a Gaming Pivot

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

NVIDIA has announced that co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO whilst continuing as CFO, with Harvey Jones becoming the board’s first-ever chair. The announcement didn’t give a reason, although it obviously arrived after very public reports of extramarital affairs, one of them reportedly with a woman US intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. Neither NVIDIA nor Huang has confirmed the reporting, but investors reacted regardless, with shares falling as much as 14% at the open.

Masato Kumzawa addresses fan reactions to Grace Ashcroft's design and the impact of NVIDIA's DLSS 5 AI technology.

Ultimately, I’m not that interested in the gossip. What interests me far more is what happens to a company that has spent the last few years being defined by one man’s bet on AI, and whether that opens the door for the side of the business that first made NVIDIA a household name. For anyone who has tried to buy a graphics card recently, that is a rather important question.

Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993 and ran it for more than 33 years, with the move into AI being very much his decision. It has paid off enormously, because data centres now make up roughly 91.5% of the company’s revenue. The flip side is that nobody else has been quite as closely tied to that strategy, which makes for some interesting possibilities for NVIDIA’s future.

Kress has been CFO since 2013 and is a well-respected voice with the market, and eToro’s Josh Gilbert described her as a familiar and trusted presence, whilst adding that a company known for its technical edge might want an engineer in the chair. Analyst Dan Ives expects her stint as interim CEO to last around a year before NVIDIA looks outside. NVIDIA’s company structure is interesting in that it doesn’t make finding a solution any easier: Huang had more than 60 people reporting to him directly.

NVIDIA has no COO, and reports suggest there was no succession plan in place. The internal names analysts have put forward, such as Ian Buck, Bill Dally, Michael Kagan and Bryan Catanzaro, are largely AI and data centre figures, but none of them has been the face of the strategy in the way Huang was. Constellation Research’s Ray Wang pointed out that many of NVIDIA’s partnerships and investments came about because people trusted Jensen.

Which brings me to the hopium. NVIDIA started out making graphics cards for gamers, and CNBC has pointed out that those gamers helped keep the company afloat back in 1999 by buying the GeForce 256. These days they account for under 10% of revenue, and it shows: RTX 50-series production was reportedly cut by up to 40% earlier this year, the Super refresh was reportedly shelved, and the next generation has reportedly drifted towards 2028. Meanwhile, the RTX 5090 launched at $1,999 and third-party sellers have been asking far more than that ever since.

Nvidia DLSS 5 is officially supported in 2K27, but eager fans have found their own way to enable the software in a myriad of titles.

So it isn’t hard to see why some gamers are hoping the board promotes someone with roots on that side of the business. Jeff Fisher, SVP of GeForce, has been at NVIDIA since 1994, but it is obvious that Kress is probably the safer bet for investors. Jonah Alben, who has led GPU engineering since 2008, and co-founder Chris Malachowsky might also throw a hat into this race. It is however important to note that all of this is still very much speculation: nobody at NVIDIA has hinted at a gaming pivot, and whether that will happen with any likeliness will be heavily dependent on other factors.

Truth be told, I wouldn’t expect a new CEO to change much straight away, even one with a soft spot for gaming. The memory shortage squeezing GeForce is affecting the entire industry, with Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron reportedly prioritising AI customers for their high-bandwidth memory, and that won’t disappear because of who is sitting in the corner office.

Whoever takes over will also inherit a company that has just lost its founder and a fair amount of investor confidence, which tends to make boards cautious rather than adventurous. Even so, I’d quite like to see someone in charge who remembers where GeForce came from, and who has some sympathy for the people still trying to buy one. For now, Kress is running both the company and its finances whilst the search for a permanent CEO gets under way.

#4308. A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

A promising new approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

"We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic."

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

Applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

The researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

But the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly important for developing faster and more compact computer components.

"Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout."

In other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A New Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly important goal.

Caretta believes the new findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

It also shows that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta said. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us."

The research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

#4307. Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.

#4306. Legendary game creator Vince Zampella has passed away

Vince Zampella, co-creator of Call of Duty, and a veteran studio head responsible for some of the biggest franchises in the world, is gone.

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

According to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

“While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he showed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”

#4305. KRÜ Blaze win Game Changers Championship from lower bracket, ending Gentle Mates’ unbeaten run

KRÜ Blaze came through the lower bracket to beat Europe's Gentle Mates GC over five maps in São Paulo, giving LATAM its first Game Changers Championship title. They are also the last winners of the standalone event, as next year's final moves to Champions.

KRÜ Blaze are the 2026 VALORANT Game Changers Championship winners. They edged Gentle Mates GC 3-2 at the Riot Games Arena in São Paulo on 1 November. No Latin American team had lifted the title before. No team had ever won it from the lower bracket either.

The event ran from 22 October, with 10 teams competing. Gentle Mates earned US$100,000 as runners-up. Shopify Rebellion Gold took US$70,000 for third place and MIBR GC US$50,000 for fourth.

KRÜ took the long route. They beat Gen.G GC 2-1 in the upper-bracket quarter-finals on 23 October. A 2-0 loss to Shopify Rebellion Gold on 27 October then dropped them into the lower bracket. They answered with clean sweeps of Team Liquid Brazil and MIBR GC. On 31 October they beat Shopify Rebellion Gold 3-1 in the best-of-five lower-bracket final.

The grand final swung back and forth. Gentle Mates took Haven 13-5 before KRÜ levelled on Abyss by the same score. KRÜ led the third map 10-2 at half-time. Gentle Mates fought back, but KRÜ closed it out 14-12 in overtime. Gentle Mates then won Split 13-8 to force a decider. KRÜ led 11-5 on Ascent and won it by the same margin as Split.

Liquipedia named KRÜ’s Argentine player tok1o as the event’s MVP. Brazilian teammates antG and none became the first Brazilians to win an international tournament held in São Paulo.

The result breaks a pattern. Before 2026 the title went to G2 Gozen for Europe in 2022, Shopify Rebellion for North America in 2023 and 2024, and Team Liquid Brazil in 2025. KRÜ’s own record at the event had improved steadily. They finished 7th–8th in 2022 and 5th–6th in each of the next two years. Last year they came fourth.

For European fans, it was a painful near miss. Gentle Mates GC arrived as EMEA’s top seed on circuit points. The team had not lost a series in São Paulo before the final, according to Esports News UK.

It capped a strong debut season in the circuit. Gentle Mates won EMEA Stage 1 by sweeping G2 Gozen 3-0 on 22 February. They lost the Stage 2 final to SK Nebula on 24 May without winning a map. On 30 August they lost the Stage 3 final to G2 Gozen in a fifth map. Silver in São Paulo leaves them with one title from four finals this year.

After a lower bracket run in São Paulo, the LATAM squad claimed the #VCTGameChangers Championship trophy! pic.twitter.com/YeSeb10TZc

— VCT Pacific (@vctpacific) November 1, 2026

The São Paulo final also closes a format. KRÜ are the last team to lift the trophy at a separate event of its own. For the first time, the Game Changers Championship will finish at Champions. Under Riot’s 2027 plan, non-partner teams that qualify for the Game Changers Championship will receive an extra US0,000 incentive. VALORANT Champions 2027 is scheduled for 16 September to 10 October in Austin.

#4304. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors

Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
